newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil leader comes out fighting against scandal.
newsitem.headline: Brazil leader comes out fighting against scandal.

text.p: Boosted by a positive Senate vote on his bid for re-election in 1998, Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso came out fighting on Thursday against a money-for-votes scandal and his slipping popularity.
Blasting the opposition for trying to misuse the alleged scam to paralyse urgent fiscal reforms in Congress, Cardoso vowed that those guilty of corruption would be punished.

"The most strident voices of the opposition are taking advantage of the lack of decorum of a few congressmen to try and paralyse Congress and the government through suspicious insinuations," the president said in a speech.
"If someone in the government is involved in this episode, they will be dismissed. I don't believe it," he added.

The Brazilian government and financial markets were shaken last week after the Folha de Sao Paulo newspaper published tapes allegedly revealing that five deputies were bribed $190,000 each to vote in favour of a bill allowing re-election.
The bill would allow presidents, governors and mayors to seek a second consecutive term for the first time since the republic was established in 1889.
It was approved by the lower house in January and passed through the first of two votes in the Senate on Wednesday night.
The Senate ballot was rushed through to beat opposition attempts to set up a special Parliamentary Committee of Inquiry (CPI), which would bring all work in Congress to a standstill.

On Wednesday night, an internal congressional probe recommended impeachment of the deputies linked to the money-for-votes scam and suggested prosecutors investigate the role of the governors of Amazonas and Acre states, as well as that of Communications Minister Sergio Motta.
Cardoso had kept an unaccustomed silence since the votes scandal broke.

Observers saw Cardoso's bellicose speech as a counterattack against his slipping popularity, reflected in an IBOPE poll published on Thursday that showed the president's approval rating had plunged 20 points to 50 percent since March.
In the speech, Cardoso attacked the opposition for organising violent demonstrations in recent weeks.
Tear gas-firing police clashed with stone-throwing youths in Rio de Janeiro during the privatisation of mining giant CVRD.
In Brasilia, rural workers invaded the office of Planning Minister Antonio Kandir and planted a turkey on his chair.
And during a hemispheric free trade meeting in Belo Horizonte, hundreds of masked protesters bearing communist party banners burnt the U.S. flag and shouted abuse at Cardoso.

"The premeditated wave of violence and anarchy is not only an attack on democracy, it's an attack on the hope of the Brazilian people, which is based on economic stability and also on political stability," Cardoso said.

Cardoso thanked the Senate for approving re-election and implored congressmen to support his reforms of the civil service and pensions system, which he said were both essential for Brazil's fiscal health.

"Every sector of Brazilian politics will have to assume responsibility in front of the people and history for the votes they gave the reforms, which we will push through because Brazil needs them," he said.
